title: Oliver Twist
full_review:
If Charles Dickens were alive today, and had royalties from all the stage, film and television adaptations of "Oliver Twist" (TriStar), he'd be as wealthy as the queen herself.

And he would almost surely give a thumbs-up to this fine and handsome new version, in spite of some reasonable streamlining of the narrative, and the elimination of some of the coincidental plot turns Victorian readers so loved.

There can scarcely be anyone who doesn't know the basic story of the foundling boy Oliver (Barney Clark) who, after daring to ask for "more" at the horrific workhouse at which he is lodged, apprentices for a funeral director, suffers abuse, runs away to London and is taken under the wing of the streetwise pickpocket known as the Artful Dodger (Harry Eden), who recruits him to join the lost boys gang headed by their Jewish ringleader, the elderly Fagin (Ben Kingsley).

Oliver's first criminal outing, where he observes the Artful Dodger and another boy pick the pocket of a prominent gentleman, Mr. Brownlow (Edward Hardwicke), at a storefront bookstall, goes awry. Oliver is the presumed culprit, and is dragged into court, but Brownlow -- sensing the boy's inherent goodness -- takes him in to raise him as his own.

Fagin and his cohorts, including the brutish Bill Sykes (Jamie Foreman), fear Oliver will snitch to the authorities, and they coerce Bill's girl, Nancy (Leanne Rowe), tough but with a heart of gold, to kidnap the boy back again -- which, against her better judgment, she does. She later tries to make amends by helping Oliver escape, and pays dearly. (In his lifetime, Dickens would give dramatic readings of his works in his public appearances, and Nancy's murder was one of his favorites.)

The movie goes wrong only near the end when young Oliver demands he be allowed to visit Fagin in prison. The scene -- though derived from the book -- feels out of place, and Kingsley's hammy hysterics undercut what had been a finely judged performance till then: the Fagin of one's dreams. He doesn't overdo the Semitic aspects of the part that have been so decried over the years. Almost unrecognizable at first in his wizened beard and with an obsequious manner, you feel he cares about the boys, despite the unlawful uses through which he exploits them.

Clark makes a good Oliver, and Eden's Dodger is reminiscent of Jack Wild in the 1968 movie musical. There's an especially colorful turn by Mark Strong as Toby Crackit, one of Fagin's cronies.

Director Roman Polanski knows how to do right by the classics ("Macbeth," "Tess") and, abridgements notwithstanding, has kept in all the essentials. For a more complete account, you need one of the British TV series that have surfaced over here on public television.

All the roles are beautifully performed by a top-notch cast. If there's a quibble, it's perhaps something of a lack in some of the smaller parts. Alun Armstrong's bumbling magistrate, for instance, simply isn't as funny as it should be. (Where are the splendid character actors of old?)

Ronald Harwood, who adapted Dickens' tale, has streamlined the original, dropping some familiar bits and reinstating others less frequently dramatized.

The detailed and attractive production design, with its vivid re-creation of a bustling Victorian London, is almost as lavish as the Oscar-winning musical. The ambience is a little less gloomy and darkly atmospheric than prior renderings, perhaps due to Pawel Edelman's crystalline lensing. Rachel Portman's evocative score is another asset.

Did we really need another "Oliver Twist"? Probably not, but the last big-screen version was 37 years ago, and when the results are as felicitous as this, who's counting?

There are no objectionable elements in the film, apart from the obvious villainy of the criminal characters who, in any case, get their comeuppance, and even Nancy's murder is treated with utmost discretion, and perhaps all the more horrifying for so being. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
